provenance.other: “the waters were abated” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Genesis 8:3, 8:8 and 8:11, all of the flood; “from off the face of” occurs in exactly six, of which only Genesis 8:8 puts the waters and that preposition together. Genesis 8:13, which the study apparatus cites here, reads ‘the waters were dried up from off the earth’ — the right event, the wrong preposition. “receded” occurs in no KJV verse; it is the Book of Mormon's own word.
provenance.significance: Ether's opening chapter took its people out of Genesis 11, the tower and the confounded language, and this verse takes the land they arrive at out of Genesis 8, the receding flood. The two halves of the primeval history frame the book: Moroni has Ether preach 'all things, from the beginning of man', and the sequence he preaches is the sequence of Genesis — creation, flood, dispersion — with the New World inserted at the point where the waters go down and dry land appears. The chosen land is, in the logic of the borrowing, the first land the flood uncovers.

13:2.note: 'How that after the waters had receded from off the face of this land, it became a choice land above all other lands.' The verb is not the King James Bible's but the prepositional phrase is, and it is the flood's: of the six KJV verses reading 'from off the face of', five are destructions and one, Genesis 8:8, is the dove sent out to see whether the waters had abated. The dependence is on the episode rather than on a clause — hence 'moderate', not higher — but it is not a general flood allusion: Ether 13:2 is describing the moment Genesis 8:8-13 describes, the uncovering of ground, and it reaches for Genesis's own preposition to describe it. Note that the promise attached to the land here ('the Lord would have that all men should serve him, which dwelleth upon the face thereof') is the same decree Ether 2:10 states, so the verse is folding the book's own land-covenant into the flood narrative.
13:2.text: Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground;

provenance.other: “New Jerusalem” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 3:12 and 21:2, and nowhere in the Old Testament. “cometh down out of heaven” occurs in exactly one, Revelation 3:12; Revelation 21:2 reads 'coming down from God out of heaven' and 21:10 'descending out of heaven from God'. Ether 13:3's relative clause — 'which should come down out of heaven' — has Revelation 3:12's shape without 'from God', which is the half of the phrase 3:12 also omits.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has already recorded the name at 3 Nephi 20:22 and 21:23, where the risen Christ uses it. What Ether 13:3 adds is the descent, and the descent is what makes the anachronism total: a Jaredite prophet who lives before Babel's dispersion has finished is given a term coined in the last book of the New Testament, together with the clause Revelation attaches to it. Recover Revelation 3:12's context and the borrowing gathers a second meaning — the promise there is made to a church told 'thou hast a little strength, and hast kept my word, and hast not denied my name', which is precisely the posture Moroni assigns to Ether in this chapter: a prophet whose word is kept and whose people 'esteemed him as nought' (13:13).

13:3.note: 'And that it was the place of the New Jerusalem, which should come down out of heaven, and the holy sanctuary of the Lord.' Two of the three elements are traceable to one verse. Revelation 3:12 is one of only two KJV verses to name the new Jerusalem and the only one whose relative clause reads 'which cometh down out of heaven'; Ether 13:3 keeps the relative construction and shifts the tense to the future the prophecy needs. The third element, 'the holy sanctuary of the Lord', is not from Revelation — 'sanctuary of the LORD' occurs in exactly five KJV verses and none of them is eschatological — and it is what makes the sentence a Jaredite one rather than a Johannine one: the city descends and it is a temple. The chapter then does something Revelation does not, which is to give the descending city an address on a continent.
13:3.text: Him that overcometh will I make a pillar in the temple of my God, and he shall go no more out: and I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, which is new Jerusalem, which cometh down out of heaven from my God: and I will write upon him my new name.

provenance.other: “the holy city” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses — Nehemiah 11:1 and 11:18, Isaiah 48:2 and 52:1, Matthew 4:5 and 27:53, Revelation 11:2, 21:2 and 22:19. Only one of them addresses Jerusalem as the holy city in a promise of restoration after destruction, and that is Isaiah 52:1. “put on thy strength” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:1-2 is quoted outright elsewhere in the Book of Mormon, at 3 Nephi 20:36 and again in Moroni's last chapter; it is the passage the book uses for Jerusalem's rebuilding. So this verse's 'built up again a holy city unto the Lord' is not reaching for a fresh source but for the one the corpus has already settled on, and the argument of Ether 13:4-8 is built by setting it against Revelation's city: the old Jerusalem gets Isaiah's promise, the new one gets John's, and verse 5 exists to say that the two are not the same city.

13:5.note: 'The Jerusalem from whence Lehi should come; after that it should be destroyed, it should be built up again a holy city unto the Lord.' The verbal contact is one phrase widely spread across the KJV, so the row is recorded at moderate and not above. What earns it is the discrimination the verse is performing: Moroni has just used Revelation's 'New Jerusalem' and now stops to rule out the obvious misreading — 'wherefore it could not be a New Jerusalem, for it had been in a time of old'. The old city he keeps is Isaiah's, the KJV's one address to Jerusalem as a holy city to be raised after ruin, and the Book of Mormon quotes that address at length in two other books. Recorded so that a reader who arrives here from 3 Nephi 20:36 is told the catalogue saw the same passage standing behind the phrase.
13:5.whyNot: 'Holy city' is nine KJV verses and 'built up' is common; nothing in Ether 13:5 reproduces a clause of Isaiah 52:1, and the sentence can be accounted for as the Book of Mormon's own idiom for restoration. The row rests on which of the nine verses fits, not on the words themselves.
13:5.text: Awake, awake; put on thy strength, O Zion; put on thy beautiful garments, O Jerusalem, the holy city: for henceforth there shall no more come into thee the uncircumcised and the unclean.

provenance.route: Genesis 46:1-7 and 49:33 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “brought his father” and “he died there” occur in no KJV verse; there is no clause here to count. Genesis 46:4 is the single verse of the descent narrative that contains both halves of Ether's sentence — the going down into Egypt and the death there, the latter in the idiom 'Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes'. Genesis 49:33 is where Jacob actually dies.
provenance.significance: The text announces its own figure — 'for the which things there has been a type' — which is unusual enough to be worth saying plainly: this is one of the few places in the Book of Mormon where a typological reading is not the catalogue's inference but the text's instruction. The type is exact in its structure and inverted in its direction. Joseph brings his father down into a foreign land and the father dies there, and the mercy consists in his not perishing before he arrives; the Lord brings a remnant of Joseph's seed out of Jerusalem to a foreign land, and the mercy is the same word twice, 'that they should perish not'. Genesis's descent preserves a family in exile; Ether's exodus preserves a family for an inheritance. The New Jerusalem of verses 6 and 8 is what the antitype gets that the type did not.

13:7.note: 'For as Joseph brought his father down into the land of Egypt, even so he died there; wherefore the Lord brought a remnant of the seed of Joseph out of the land of Jerusalem.' No clause is reproduced and none needs to be: the verse is a declared typology, marked as such in verse 6, and it is adjudicated as figural on the strength of its structure rather than its wording. Genesis 46:4 is the verse that holds the whole of the type in one sentence, God's promise to Jacob that he will go down with him into Egypt and that Joseph will close his eyes there. Note that our extract of the study apparatus keys Genesis 46:1-7 to this verse but drops the second half of its own note, which reads 'Gen 46.1–7; 49.33' on the page — and 49:33 is the verse that supplies 'even so he died there'. Recorded at high because the text asserts the figure and the figure holds at every point.
13:7.text: I will go down with thee into Egypt; and I will also surely bring thee up again: and Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes.

provenance.other: “confound” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, of which Genesis 11:7 and 11:9 are the tower; “did there confound” occurs in exactly one, Genesis 11:9. The passive 'confounded' is common in the KJV — 47 verses — and almost always means 'put to shame', which is not what it means here. The sense required at Ether 13:8 is Genesis 11's active one, and it is the sense Ether 1:33-35 has already established for the book.
provenance.significance: This is the book closing its own circle, and the circle is a KJV one. Ether opens at Genesis 11: Jared and his brother come 'from the great tower, at the time the Lord confounded the language of the people', and 1:35 records that 'Jared and his brother were not confounded'. Thirteen chapters later the same verb returns in the promise that the seed of Joseph 'shall no more be confounded, until the end come'. The Jaredites are, by their own founding story, the people who escaped the confounding once; the prophecy Ether is given is that the confounding ends for good in a city built on the land they were brought to. Genesis 11:9's second half — 'from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth' — is the sentence Ether 1:33 also borrows for the scattering, so both halves of Babel are in the book's first chapter and both are answered in its thirteenth.

13:8.note: 'And they shall build up a holy city unto the Lord, like unto the Jerusalem of old; and they shall no more be confounded, until the end come, when the earth shall pass away.' “shall no more be confounded” occurs in no KJV verse, and read as ordinary King James English 'confounded' would mean put to shame — which is how it reads to anyone who has not been through Ether 1. Read against the book's own opening it means the other thing. The mediation field carries the argument: the proximate model is not Genesis 11:9 directly but Ether 1:33-35, which is where Genesis 11's active 'confound' enters this book, and 13:8 is answering that verse rather than the chapter of Genesis. Recorded at moderate because the single shared word is doing all the work; what makes it worth a row is that no other reading of the word makes sense of the sentence.
13:8.whyNot: One word, and a common one in the KJV in a different sense. A reader may reasonably take 'confounded' here as Isaiah 45:17's 'ye shall not be ashamed nor confounded world without end', which fits the eschatological frame and requires no Babel at all.
13:8.text: Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:17 → Revelation 21:1 (with 2 Corinthians 5:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 65:17 reads plural throughout — 'I create new heavens and a new earth' — and its second clause is 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind'.
provenance.other: “a new heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 21:1. “new heavens and a new earth” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 65:17 and 2 Peter 3:13, both plural. “old things are passed away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “all things are become new” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, 2 Corinthians 5:17.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points and both favour Revelation 21:1 over Isaiah 65:17: the Book of Mormon has the singular 'heaven' where Isaiah has 'heavens', and it has the passing-away clause where Isaiah has 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind'. 2 Peter 3:13 is ruled out on the same singular/plural test.
provenance.significance: The verse is a seam between two New Testament passages that are not otherwise joined, and the seam is visible in one sentence. Its first half is Revelation 21:1, the cosmological new creation seen by a seer; its second half is 2 Corinthians 5:17, where the new creation is a person — 'if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new'. Both of Paul's clauses are KJV singletons and both are here. What the fusion produces is a doctrine neither verse states: that the new heaven and new earth 'shall be like unto the old, save the old have passed away', a continuity Revelation 21:1 explicitly denies by adding 'and there was no more sea'. The Book of Mormon has taken John's cosmos and Paul's grammar of renewal and used the second to soften the first.

13:9.note: 'And there shall be a new heaven and a new earth; and they shall be like unto the old, save the old have passed away, and all things have become new.' Seven words in order from a KJV singleton, then both surviving clauses of a second. The mediation is the finding. Isaiah 65:17 is the ultimate source and the Book of Mormon does not have Isaiah's form of it: Isaiah writes 'new heavens' and the singular 'a new heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse in the whole Bible. Since the verse is transmitted through the New Testament it is recorded as OT-via-NT rather than direct-OT, which is the same test that decided 1 Nephi 22:20 and 3 Nephi 5:24. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations, but the fusion is tighter than a threshold measures — three of the four elements are KJV singletons.
13:9.text: And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea.

provenance.other: “white in the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “washed their robes” occurs in exactly one, both Revelation 7:14. “the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly two, Revelation 7:14 and 12:11. “blessed are they” occurs in exactly twelve, of which Revelation 19:9 — 'Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb' — is the one that pairs the formula with the Lamb.
provenance.alternative: The mediation is genuinely unsettled and the enum has no value for its likeliest shape. Revelation 7:14 reads 'made them white IN the blood of the Lamb'; Ether 13:10 reads 'white THROUGH the blood of the Lamb', which is not the KJV's preposition but is the Book of Mormon's — Alma 13:11, 'their garments were washed white, through the blood of the Lamb', and Alma 5:21, 'through the blood of him of whom it hath been spoken'. So the proximate model is probably an earlier Book of Mormon passage rather than the KJV page, exactly as with an OT source reaching a verse through an earlier Nephite quotation. The schema offers OT-via-earlier-BoM and nothing for a New Testament source arriving the same way, so this row is filed direct-NT and the route is stated here rather than in a sixth invented value. Flagged for the schema, not resolved by it.
provenance.significance: Revelation 7:13-14 is a dialogue in which an interlocutor asks who the white-robed are and the seer is told: 'These are they which came out of great tribulation.' The Book of Mormon has been answering that question in its own terms since 1 Nephi 12:11, and Ether 13:10-11 gives the answer a geography. The white-robed of the New Jerusalem are 'numbered among the remnant of the seed of Joseph'; the white-robed of the old Jerusalem, one verse later, are the scattered of Israel gathered back. John's undifferentiated multitude out of every nation has been sorted into two cities, and the sorting principle is descent.

13:10.note: 'For it is they whose garment are white through the blood of the Lamb; and they are they which are numbered among the remnant of the seed of Joseph.' Revelation 7:14 supplies both halves of the identification: the whitened garments in the Lamb's blood, which is a KJV singleton, and the demonstrative formula for naming who the whitened are. The 1830 reading is the singular 'garment', corrected to 'garments' in 1920 — which is worth flagging because 'garments' is the KJV's word and the first edition does not have it. The preposition is likewise not Revelation's: 'through' rather than 'in', which is the Book of Mormon's own settled form of the phrase by Alma 13:11 and is why the mediation note above is unresolved.
13:10.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.route: Genesis 22:18 → Acts 3:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the covenant which God made” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 3:25. Genesis has no such phrase: at 17:7 the covenant is 'established', at 15:18 the LORD 'made a covenant with Abram', and neither wording is this one.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point: the Book of Mormon stops where Acts 3:25 stops and does not carry Genesis 22:18's closing clause, 'because thou hast obeyed my voice'. The relative construction with 'God' as subject is Acts's and not Genesis's.
provenance.significance: Acts 3:25 is Peter telling the men of Israel in Solomon's porch that they are the children of the covenant, and the catalogue has recorded the Book of Mormon reaching for that verse three times before, always for the Abrahamic promise to a scattered Israel. Ether 13:11 is the strangest of the four contexts, because the speaker is not an Israelite: Moroni is reporting a Jaredite prophecy about the old Jerusalem, and the covenant language he uses for it is a Petrine sermon's. Recover the context and the metalepsis is sharper still — Peter's next words are the promise that God will send Jesus Christ 'whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things', which is what Ether 13:9-11 has just spent three verses describing.

13:11.note: 'And are partakers of the fulfilling of the covenant which God made with their father Abraham.' Seven consecutive words — 'of the covenant which God made with' — reproducing a KJV singleton, and the singleton is a New Testament verse quoting Genesis. That makes it a mediation case rather than a straightforward Old Testament borrowing, and the diff decides it cleanly: Acts 3:25 ends the promise at the blessing of the kindreds of the earth, Genesis 22:18 continues 'because thou hast obeyed my voice', and the Book of Mormon has Acts's shorter form. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations.
13:11.text: Ye are the children of the prophets, and of the covenant which God made with our fathers, saying unto Abraham, And in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed.

provenance.other: “the four quarters of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:8. Isaiah 11:12, the gathering prophecy this sentence is otherwise reciting, reads 'the four corners of the earth'; Jeremiah 49:36 has 'the four quarters of heaven'.
provenance.significance: By Ether the phrase is a Book of Mormon idiom and the row is calibrated accordingly — the argument for it was made at 1 Nephi 19:16 and again at 3 Nephi 5:24, and it is not remade here. What the recurrence adds is its reach: the same KJV singleton, taken from the mustering of Gog and Magog and used for the gathering of Israel, has now appeared in four books and three hands. A borrowing that survives that many redactional layers is either the corpus's own formula or a habit of the English behind all of them, and the catalogue cannot tell those apart from inside the text.

13:11.note: 'And they are they which were scattered and gathered in from the four quarters of the earth.' The link is written rather than excluded because Ether is a new book and a reader who meets the phrase here should be told where it comes from; the argument itself belongs to 1 Nephi 19:16, where the substitution of Revelation's 'quarters' for Isaiah 11:12's 'corners' was first adjudicated. Recorded at moderate, as at 3 Nephi 20:13, on the ground that 'gathered in from the four quarters' is by this point a standing Book of Mormon idiom and the verse can be accounted for without any KJV page open.
13:11.whyNot: The phrase has become the corpus's own; five words shared with Revelation 20:8 prove dependence somewhere in the book's history but not at this verse. The contexts are also opposed — Revelation 20:8 gathers the nations to battle, Ether 13:11 gathers Israel to a covenant.
13:11.text: And shall go out to deceive the nations which are in the four quarters of the earth, Gog, and Magog, to gather them together to battle: the number of whom is as the sand of the sea.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 31:8 (with 16:15 and 23:8) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “north countries” occurs in no KJV verse; the King James Bible has the singular “the north country” in exactly eight, six of them Jeremiah. “the coasts of the earth” occurs in exactly three, of which Jeremiah 31:8 is the one that pairs it with the north country and a gathering. Jeremiah 23:8 supplies the other half of Ether's clause, 'the seed of the house of Israel out of the north country, and from all countries whither I had driven them'.
provenance.alternative: The printed study apparatus keys 'the lost tribes; see Jer 15.16; 31.8' to this verse. Jeremiah 15:16 is 'Thy words were found, and I did eat them' and has no contact with a gathering from the north at any point; Jeremiah 16:15 is 'The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north', which is exactly what the note says it is citing. The likeliest account is a transposition of digits in the printed apparatus — 16.15 for 15.16 — of the same class as the 2 Nephi 17:17 citation already recorded in data/hardy-corrections.json. Separately, our own extract of the note dropped its second reference, 31.8, keeping only the first; that is a fact about our parser, and the same truncation shows at Ether 13:7.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 31 is the new-covenant chapter, and verse 8 is the gathering that precedes it: 'I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame.' Ether 13:11 sets that gathering beside the covenant with Abraham in a single sentence, so the old Jerusalem's restoration is given both of the Bible's covenants at once — the one made with the father and the one Jeremiah says will be new. Neither text says this; the sentence does.

13:11.note: 'And from the north countries' — the Book of Mormon's plural against the King James Bible's consistent singular, which is why this is an echo and not an allusion. The referent is not in doubt: a gathering of Israel from the north is Jeremiah's subject at 16:15, 23:8 and 31:8, and 31:8 is the only one that also gathers from the ends of the earth, which is what Ether's preceding clause does. Recorded so that the study apparatus's cross-reference here is discharged with a verse that actually bears it; see the exclusion register at 13:11 for why the printed citation cannot be right.
13:11.whyNot: No clause is shared and the one distinctive noun is in the wrong number. A reader may fairly say the Book of Mormon has a general biblical idea of the northern captivity and no particular verse of Jeremiah in view.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Ether 13.11 (the lost tribes; Jer 15.16; 31.8)
13:11.text: Behold, I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth, and with them the blind and the lame, the woman with child and her that travaileth with child together: a great company shall return thither.

provenance.other: “which shall be last” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “which shall be first” occurs in exactly one, and they are the same verse, Luke 13:30. Matthew 19:30 and Mark 10:31 read 'many that are first shall be last'; Matthew 20:16 reads 'So the last shall be first, and the first last'. Only Luke has the relative pronoun, and only Luke has the existential 'there are'.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for Luke over Matthew 19:30, but the evidence is genuinely split and the split is worth stating. The syntax is Luke's twice over — 'there are they which ... which shall be' reproduces Luke 13:30's construction, and both of its halves are KJV singletons. The ORDER is not Luke's: Luke runs last-then-first, and Ether 13:12 runs first-then-last, which is Matthew 19:30's and Mark 10:31's sequence. So the verse has Luke's words in Matthew's arrangement, and the row is filed at Luke because the words are the harder evidence.
provenance.significance: 'And when these things come, bringeth to pass the Scripture which saith' — a Jaredite prophecy is here said to fulfil 'the scripture', and the scripture in question is a saying of Jesus recorded in Luke, in wording that did not exist in English until 1611. This is the availability criterion failing in the most concentrated form the catalogue has met in Ether: not an echo that could be unconscious but an explicit citation formula pointing at a text that, on the book's own chronology, is two thousand years in its future. The metalepsis is worth recovering as well. Luke 13:30 closes the passage about the strait gate, where many will seek to enter and shall not be able, and where those who come 'from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south' sit down in the kingdom while the householder's own acquaintances are shut out — which is precisely the sorting Ether 13:10-11 has just performed between the seed of Joseph and the Jerusalem of old.

13:12.note: 'There are they which were first, which shall be last; and there are they which were last, which shall be first.' Two KJV singletons in one sentence, and both belong to Luke 13:30. The catalogue has adjudicated the same saying once before, at 1 Nephi 13:42, where the wording was Matthew 20:16's most regular English form; this is a different form of the same logion and the difference is diagnostic — Ether has the relative pronouns and the existential that only Luke has. The 1830 text reads 'which' at all four points where 1920 reads 'who', which preserves the KJV's own relative and makes the borrowing plainer in the first edition than in the current one. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his quotations.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Ether 13.12 (Matt 19.30; Mark 10.31; Luke 13.30)
13:12.text: And, behold, there are last which shall be first, and there are first which shall be last.

provenance.other: “I was about to write” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 10:4. The catalogue has already used that verse at Ether 4:5, but for its second half — 'seal up those things' — rather than its first; this is where the first half arrives, verbatim.
provenance.significance: Revelation 10:4 is the seer stopped mid-transcription: the seven thunders speak, John lifts his pen, and a voice from heaven forbids him to write what he heard. Moroni's chapter does the same thing at the same point in its own argument, and the parallel is structural, not just verbal — both prohibitions fall immediately after a vision of the new Jerusalem and immediately before the seer turns to the destruction of a people. The prohibition is also the book's own recurring gesture: Ether 4:5 sealed a record up, Ether 12:24 confessed the weakness of writing, and here the writing simply stops. Compare 3 Nephi 26:11, where Mormon reports the same interdiction — but the 1830 text there reads 'Behold I were about to write them all ... but the Lord forbid it', and 'I were' is in no KJV verse. Moroni's clause is the one that matches the singleton exactly.

13:13.note: 'And I was about to write more, but I am forbidden.' Six words reproducing a KJV singleton, and the situation reproduced with them: a seer interrupted in the act of writing by a prohibition he does not explain. The Book of Mormon's version compresses Revelation's — John hears a voice and is told what not to write, Moroni simply says he is forbidden — but the compression keeps the one clause that is unique to Revelation 10:4 in the whole English Bible. Recorded as an allusion rather than a quotation because the reproduced run stops at six words and the rest of the verse goes its own way; below Skousen's threshold and not one of his quotations.
13:13.text: And when the seven thunders had uttered their voices, I was about to write: and I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Seal up those things which the seven thunders uttered, and write them not.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and in no Old Testament verse in that form. The 1830 text preserves the KJV's double-l spelling, 'marvellous'; 1920 modernized it to 'marvelous', so the borrowing is visible on the page of the first edition and not on the page of the current one.
provenance.significance: The pairing entered the Book of Mormon at 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi's praise reproduces six words of Revelation 15:3 and the catalogue reads the echo metaleptically — Revelation labels those words 'the song of Moses ... and the song of the Lamb'. Here at the far end of the corpus the same adjective pair is spent not on God's works but on a rejected prophet's prophecies, and immediately before the sentence that says his hearers 'esteemed him as nought, and cast him out'. Revelation 15:1's great and marvellous sign is the seven angels with the seven last plagues; Ether's great and marvellous prophecies are followed in this book by the annihilation of a nation. Neither text draws that line.

13:13.note: 'But great and marvellous were the prophecies of Ether, but they esteemed him as nought, and cast him out.' The phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in one chapter of Revelation, and the 1830 spelling is the King James one. Recorded at moderate and as an echo rather than an allusion, because by Ether the pair is a standing Book of Mormon formula and the row is written for a reader of this book rather than to re-argue what was settled at 1 Nephi 1:14. What is worth noticing is the reversal: the corpus's first use praises God with it, its last narrative use applies it to a prophet nobody listened to.
13:13.whyNot: Two ordinary adjectives in a common conjunction, and one of the most-used formulas in the Book of Mormon by this point in the text. Nothing else of Revelation 15 is present at this verse.
13:13.text: And I saw another sign in heaven, great and marvellous, seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.

provenance.other: “every man did that which was right in his own eyes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Judges 17:6 and 21:25; “no king in Israel” occurs in exactly four, all of them Judges. Ether 13:25 shares none of that wording: it reads 'every man with his band, fighting for that which he desired'. The row is filed as figural for that reason and not as a verbal link.
provenance.significance: Judges' refrain is the King James Bible's one formula for a society that has come apart because there is no king, and it is spoken over a book that ends in civil war between the tribes of Israel. Ether 13-15 is the same shape run to its end: the kingdom is contested by Coriantumr, Shared, and after them Gilead, Lib and Shiz; the land divides into bands; and by 15:2 two million have fallen. The difference is the one the catalogue should not smooth over. Judges says there was no king, and Ether's anarchy is caused by there being too many claimants to one — the verse before this records the kingdom changing hands twice in two years. Ether 13:31's 'there was none to constrain them' is the closest the chapter comes to Judges' diagnosis, and it names an absent restraint rather than an absent king.

13:25.note: 'Now there began to be a war upon all the face of the land, every man with his band, fighting for that which he desired.' No clause is shared and the row is written as figural on that basis. What it records is that the King James Bible has exactly one way of narrating a nation dissolving into private violence — the Judges refrain, twice at 17:6 and 21:25 and echoed at 18:1 and 19:1 — and that Ether 13:25 constructs the same sentence out of its own vocabulary: a distributive 'every man', a private object of desire, and no authority in the frame. Recorded at moderate because the pattern is strong and the wording will not carry it; a reader who sees Judges here should be told the catalogue saw it too and declined to call it verbal dependence.
13:25.whyNot: Not one distinctive word is shared, and civil collapse narrated as 'every man' doing as he pleases is available to any English writer without Judges. If the wording is the test, this row fails it; it is kept because the exclusion register would lose the observation.
13:25.text: In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.

provenance.other: “and there was none to” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Deuteronomy 22:27, 2 Samuel 14:6, Psalm 79:3, Psalm 107:12 and Isaiah 63:5. Only one of them completes the clause with a burial, and only one has blood shed in the same sentence: Psalm 79:3, “Their blood have they shed”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. “none to bury” occurs in exactly three, Psalm 79:3 among them. The 1830 text reads 'constrain' where 1920 reads 'restrain'; neither is the Psalm's word.
provenance.significance: Ten verses earlier the Lord has told Coriantumr that everyone he knows will die and that he alone will live 'to see the fulfilling of the prophecies ... and Coriantumr should receive a burial by them' — by another people, because his own will not be there to do it. Psalm 79 is the one place in the King James Bible where those two facts stand in a single verse: blood shed like water round about Jerusalem, and no one left to bury the dead. The chapter's closing sentence and its central prophecy are the two halves of Psalm 79:3, split across ten verses, and the book spends its last two chapters demonstrating them. Ether 15:33 is where the demonstration finishes: Coriantumr alone, and a people he cannot bury.

13:31.note: 'All the people upon all the face of the land were a shedding blood, and there was none to constrain them.' The construction is the KJV's — a clause of slaughter closed by 'and there was none to' plus an infinitive — and of the five verses that use it, Psalm 79:3 is the only one whose slaughter is a shedding of blood and whose missing office is burial. The Book of Mormon substitutes restraint for burial, which is why this is an echo rather than an allusion; but it has already supplied the burial itself at 13:21, in a prophecy that exists to say who will not be alive to perform one. Recorded at moderate: the shared frame is real, the shared words are five and ordinary.
13:31.whyNot: The one distinctive element of Psalm 79:3, 'none to bury them', is not in this verse, and the five-word frame that is shared is common enough that Isaiah 63:5 or Psalm 107:12 would serve as well if the sense did not decide it. The argument rests on 13:21 supplying what 13:31 lacks, which is a reading of the chapter rather than of the clause.
13:31.text: Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.
